newsitem.title: FRANCE: Politics, not decimals, to dictate EMU - Juppe.
newsitem.headline: Politics, not decimals, to dictate EMU - Juppe.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, in one of his strongest statements on the issue to date, has said European monetary union would be driven by a sense of history and not by a narrow view of the Maastricht criteria.
In an interview with the financial daily Les Echos, Juppe said he wanted Spain and Italy to take part in the first round of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) if they meet the criteria.

"Everyone in the (centre-right) majority has always been deeply sure that the decision would be a political one and that the nth decimal place could give way to historic and political considerations," Juppe told Les Echos. It released an advance copy of the interview, which will be published on Thursday.
France has insisted that countries wishing to join EMU should stick to a Maastricht treaty criterion limiting budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year.
But the opposition Socialists, campaigning ahead of a two-round parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1, have argued for a flexible interpretation of the treaty.
Juppe said the euro common currency should bring stability and growth.
"That implies as President (Jacques) Chirac often says, the participation of as many countries as possible which meet the criteria, including Italy and Spain."
Juppe said the 15-member European Union's economic policy should be oriented towards growth and should not simply be determined by the central bank.
"Obviously exchange rate parities, in particular against the dollar and the yen, must not be artificial but reflect economic reality," he said.
Europe and monetary union have become a central theme in the campaign for the snap general election, which was called nearly a year early to clear the decks for EMU at the end of next year.
In recent days, the question of the three-percent-deficit target has become a political football.
Juppe has come under fire from the Socialists and Communists, who argue that he will impose further austerity measures this year so as to hit the three-percent target.
Without further corrective measures, some economists estimate that the budget deficit could overshoot.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis has repeatedly argued that the government would do everything to come in at three percent. He said earlier this month he was targeting 3.0 percent precisely.
Juppe's comments seem likely to further fuel the debate in Europe over exactly what the rules will be for monetary union.
Last week, European Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said the Maastricht Treaty convergence criteria were "reference values but only reference values".
